planting.note: Separate rooted offsets from the base of the clump and pot in gritty, fast-draining cactus mix; plant outdoors in shade to filtered light in zone 9-11, or grow as a bright-indirect-light houseplant anywhere.

directions: Pot divisions in a lean, mineral-heavy succulent mix and place in bright indirect light, since direct midday sun can scorch the leaves while deeper shade still keeps the plant healthy. Unlike the flat rosette of its better-known relative the zebra haworthia, this species stacks its thick, incurved, white-tubercled leaves in tight spiraling columns along an upright stem, giving it a distinctly architectural, almost braided look. It offsets readily from the base, quickly forming a dense clustering colony of short columns that works well in a shallow dish garden. Water only when the mix has dried out completely, and expect a summer flush of small tubular whitish flowers on a thin, wiry stalk.

planting.note: Pot rooted offsets in gritty, well-drained succulent soil; grow in bright shade to filtered light outdoors in zone 9-11 or as a low-light indoor succulent year-round.

directions: Grow in a shallow pot of gritty cactus mix in bright shade or filtered light, since this South African species is adapted to growing under scrub and rock overhangs and scorches in hot direct sun. Young plants hold their thick, rough-textured, dark green, tongue-shaped leaves in two flat opposing ranks, the distichous arrangement the species is named for, before maturing into a looser spiral rosette. It sends up a tall, arching flower stalk carrying curved, stomach-shaped, coral-pink to orange tubular blooms well above the foliage, usually in late winter or spring. Let the soil dry fully between waterings and divide offsets from the base to propagate.

planting.note: Pot offsets in gritty, well-drained succulent mix and grow in bright indirect light or open shade; suitable outdoors in zone 9-11 or as a low-light houseplant elsewhere.

directions: Grow this compact hybrid Gasteria in a shallow container of mineral succulent mix, placed in bright indirect light; it colors up more deeply in stronger light but tolerates surprisingly dim rooms better than most other succulents. Its thick, dark green, tongue-shaped leaves are densely covered in raised, pale, wart-like tubercles that give the cultivar its name and set it apart texturally from smoother-leaved Gasteria species and hybrids. It stays small and clumps readily from basal offsets, making it a popular choice for dish gardens and small pots on shaded windowsills. Water deeply only when the mix is fully dry, since it is highly prone to rot in constantly damp soil.

common_name: Whale Fin Snake Plant (Shark Fin Sansevieria)

planting.note: Divide rooted offsets from the base and pot in fast-draining succulent or cactus mix; grow outdoors in shade in zone 10-11 or as a slow-growing indoor houseplant tolerant of low light.

directions: Pot in a fast-draining cactus mix and set in bright indirect light to open shade, giving each plant enough room since it typically produces just one to a few extremely wide, paddle-shaped leaves rather than a full clump. Native to the Congo region of West Africa, its single thick, mottled dark-green leaf can grow a foot or more wide and several feet tall, making it one of the boldest single-leaf houseplant forms available and the source of its whale-fin or shark-fin nickname. It is exceptionally slow-growing and drought-tolerant, needing water only when the mix has dried out completely, and largely shrugs off the low humidity and dim light of typical home interiors. New leaves and eventual offsets emerge slowly from a thick underground rhizome, so mature specimens are prized and often propagated by division rather than grown quickly from seed.

planting.note: Divide rhizome offsets and pot in fast-draining cactus mix; grow outdoors in shade to filtered light in zone 10-11 or as an indoor houseplant tolerant of low light.

directions: Grow in a gritty, fast-draining succulent mix in bright indirect light to open shade; the leaves develop the richest coppery-red edge coloring with a bit more light but the plant still performs well in dimmer rooms. Native to coastal East Africa, it forms a low, spreading fan of long, wavy-margined, dark green leaves marked with faint silvery cross-banding and edged in reddish-copper, a pattern that gives rise to popular selections like the 'Coppertone' form. It spreads slowly by rhizome to form a loose colony rather than a tight upright clump like the common snake plant, making it useful as a textured groundcover in a shaded succulent bed in frost-free climates. Allow the soil to dry completely between waterings, since like other sansevierias it is far more likely to be lost to rot than to drought.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full shade to deep shade; hardy to around zone 7 and slow to establish, so keep evenly moist the first year.

directions: Plant rhizome divisions in humus-rich, well-drained soil in full to deep shade, watering regularly while the clump establishes and then only occasionally once mature. This Sichuan native carries narrower, more slender leaves than the common cast iron plant, each one densely peppered overall with small creamy-white spots rather than striped or blotched, giving the whole clump a speckled, starry appearance that inspired its 'Ginga' (starry sky) name. It spreads gradually by rhizome into a dense, weed-suppressing clump and holds its markings and glossy dark green color year-round in deep shade where few other perennials can compete. Like other Aspidistra it is extremely tough and low-maintenance once established, but the fine speckling is a distinct look worth siting somewhere it can be appreciated up close, such as along a shaded path.

planting.note: Divide rhizome tubers and pot in well-drained potting mix; grow outdoors in shade in zone 10-11 or as a compact low-light houseplant year-round.

directions: Pot in a well-drained mix over a bed of underground water-storing rhizomes, and place in low to bright indirect light; it is one of the few plants that genuinely thrives in office corners and windowless rooms with minimal supplemental light. 'Zenzi' is a naturally occurring compact sport of the standard ZZ plant, with the same glossy, dark green, feather-like pinnate leaves packed more tightly onto shorter, more upright and curled stems, giving a denser, rosette-like silhouette instead of the species' typical arching sprawl. Its thick rhizomes store substantial water and energy, letting it go weeks between waterings and rebound quickly from occasional neglect. Because it stays compact at maturity, it is especially well suited to small pots, tabletops, and tight shaded spaces where the full-sized species would eventually outgrow the spot.
